statement: Use the Riegel power law with its conventional exponent of 1.06 only to predict targets up to the half marathon. For marathon targets, never output the raw single-race Riegel time as the central estimate; treat it as an optimistic bound and shade it slower. Evidence shows Riegel gave marathon times at least 10 min too fast for half of runners; it does not give a correction size.
unit: km (target distance limit for single-race Riegel)
appliesTo: Recreational runners predicting from one prior race

statement: No evidence-based exponent for extending short-race results to the marathon was retrieved. Conservative default: when the only anchor is a race of 21.1 km or shorter, add a documented placeholder slowdown to the marathon estimate and widen the interval; replace it with per-athlete fitting as soon as two or more races exist. The placeholder value is an engineering assumption, not a finding.
unit: % added to Riegel marathon time (placeholder, to be calibrated by back-testing)
appliesTo: Marathon prediction from a single race of 21.1 km or shorter

statement: When two or more race results at different distances are available, fit a per-athlete model (runner-specific exponent / endurance index) instead of a fixed exponent. Marathon MSE fell from 381 (Riegel) to 228 (one race) and 208 (two races) in a recreational sample, and per-runner exponents fit better in a 165k-runner database.
appliesTo: All runners with logged race or time-trial results

statement: Include sex, age, BMI, typical weekly mileage and a tempo/interval share as covariates when predicting from limited race data; weight tempo work more for races up to the half marathon. Include sex in half-to-marathon regressions. Age category and in-race pace range were not shown to help in the Valencia regression (pace range explicitly did not).

Display marathon predictions made from a non-marathon anchor as a range whose half-width is at least the reported mean absolute error of about 6% of predicted time, widening it for a single anchor, old data, or non-road or hot conditions. Reported errors: 5.9% (half-to-marathon regression), 7.7-8.0% (CS from logs), 5.2-6.5% (CS plus durability).

Estimate critical speed from the athlete's fastest grade-adjusted efforts over about 400 m, 800 m and 5 km (distance-time slope) and use it as a pacing anchor. Do not present it as a race-time predictor with sub-8% accuracy. Training-log efforts may not be maximal, so require recent efforts and report low confidence when none are near-maximal.
appliesTo: Recreational runners with GPS training logs

statement: Use the observed marathon intensity as a fraction of CS as a descriptive prior for target pace by ability: about 93% CS at 150 min, falling to about 79% CS at 360 min (linear interpolation between). These are what runners did, not proven optima; overridden by individual durability data when available. High-decoupling athletes (index >= 1.2) ran about 82% CS and low-decoupling (< 1.1) about 88% CS.
value: 0.93 at 150 min to 0.79 at 360 min; 0.88 low-decoupling, 0.82 high-decoupling

statement: Warn when the planned first-half marathon pace exceeds about 94% of CS (and strongly when faster than CS): this was associated with higher likelihood of a >25% second-half slowdown. Also cap the opening kilometres of the race plan; no numeric start-pace cap is supported by evidence.
appliesTo: Marathon race-day pacing plans for recreational runners

statement: Compute and store a decoupling (durability) index from long runs: (%HRmax / %CS) in the late segment divided by the same in the early segment. Classify <1.1 low, 1.1 to <1.2 moderate, >=1.2 high, and use it to shade marathon and ultra predictions. That long-run decoupling matches race decoupling is untested, so flag the proxy and back-test it per athlete; heat and hydration inflate HR-based decoupling.
appliesTo: Marathon and longer; athletes with HR and pace on long runs

statement: Choose the fitting model by the efforts available: CP models only with efforts spread over about 3-30 min; power law with efforts around 1, 3, 10 min; Peronnet with about 4-20 min. Refuse a CP fit from very short efforts only. Validated extrapolation reached 60 min only; for marathon or ultra durations add a durability term and widen the interval.
unit: min (shortest to longest effort for CP fitting); validated extrapolation limit 60 min
appliesTo: Athletes with power or pace-duration data

statement: Apply a weather adjustment for marathon-range road races: about 0.9 percentage points of slowdown per 5 C WBGT for top male runners within 5-25 C WBGT (1.7% at 5-10 C to 4.5% at 20-25 C versus course record). Slower runners slowed more but no multiplier was published; as a documented placeholder, use a multiplier of 1.5 for predicted finish over 4 h. Do not extrapolate outside 5-25 C WBGT.
value: 0.9 (elite men, derived); placeholder multiplier 1.5 for >4 h finishers
unit: percentage points of finish time per 5 C WBGT

statement: For 100-mile or 161 km predictions, scale a heat penalty by the fraction of race time expected in hot hours rather than using a flat pace: the hot year averaged about 8% slower pace over 161 km in one race, with <22 h finishers slower on 12 of 14 segments versus 6 of 14 for >24 h finishers, and pace converging at night. Treat 8% as an upper-end example from one race, not a general constant.
unit: % slower average pace in a hot versus cool year (161 km, one race, n = 50)
appliesTo: Trail ultramarathons of about 100 miles; strongest for fast finishers

statement: Predict road and trail ultra finish times from the marathon personal best (r = 0.72 with 100 km time; r = -0.58 with 24 h distance) plus weekly kilometres, habitual training pace and longest long run, with a wide interval and per-athlete back-testing. No validated exponent or coefficients for ultra extrapolation exist in this corpus; do not hard-code the 24 h regression equation or the LSTM model.
appliesTo: Ultramarathon (50 km to 100 mi); male road samples only in the evidence

statement: For hilly or trail courses, convert the elevation profile to flat-equivalent effort with the Minetti cost-versus-gradient curve (cost ratio to level: about 5.6 at +45%, 0.51 at -20%, 1.15 at -45%) but cap the downhill benefit at the -20% minimum and treat the result as an upper bound on speed, since observed downhill race speeds are far below the theoretical maximum and the curve is fresh-state. Add a fatigue term for late-race slowing; its size is not established (default 0, flagged).
unit: cost ratio to level at -20% gradient (minimum credit)
appliesTo: Trail and hilly road courses; fresh-state estimate only

statement: Do not transfer a road VDOT or CS directly to trail targets. Label trail predictions lower-confidence and widen the interval with elevation gain per km. No evidence gives the multiplier; default placeholder is a road interval widened by 50%, to be calibrated by back-testing against logged trail races.
appliesTo: Trail races; any course with substantial elevation gain
